.Converting the linear system into a standard form, with $e_1$ corresponding to $\varphi$, $e_2$ corresponding to $\sigma$, and $e_3$ to $r$:

Given $\eta^* \in W$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, the first system is

$$
\begin{align*}
\partial_t (\psi + \ell(\varphi)) - \kappa \Delta \psi &= f - \rho \sigma \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\partial_t \psi - \nu \Delta \varphi + \xi + \pi(\varphi) &= \gamma \vartheta \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\xi &\in \beta(\varphi) \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\sigma(t) &\in \text{Sign}(\vartheta(t) + \alpha \varphi(t) - \eta^*) \quad \text{for a.a. } t \in (0, T) \\
\vartheta(0) &= \vartheta_0 \quad \text{and } \varphi(0) = \varphi_0.
\end{align*}
$$

The second problem, which we call Problem $(B)$ depends on a given $\varphi^* \in W$ and consists in the equations

$$
\begin{align*}
\partial_t (\vartheta + \ell(\varphi)) - \kappa \Delta \vartheta &= f \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\partial_t \varphi - \nu \Delta \varphi + \xi + \pi(\varphi) &= \gamma \vartheta - \rho \sigma \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\xi &\in \beta(\varphi) \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\sigma(t) &\in \text{Sign}(\vartheta(t) + \alpha \varphi(t) - \eta^*) \quad \text{for a.a. } t \in (0, T) \\
0 &= \vartheta_0 \quad \text{and } \varphi(0) = \varphi_0.
\end{align*}
$$

The last case, termed Problem $(C)$, is the same as the previous one with the following difference: the non-local operator Sign is replaced by the local sign: $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow 2^{\mathbb{R}}$ defined by

$$
\sin \varphi := \frac{r}{|r|} \quad \text{if } r \neq 0 \quad \text{and } \sin \varphi_0 := [-1, 1].
$$

Notice that sign is the subdifferential of the real function $r \mapsto |r|$ and thus is maximal monotone. For the sake of clarity, we write Problem $(C)$, explicitly. Given $\varphi^* \in W$, we look for a quadruplet $(\vartheta, \varphi, \xi, \sigma)$ satisfying

$$
\begin{align*}
\partial_t (\vartheta + \ell(\varphi)) - \kappa \Delta \vartheta &= f \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\partial_t \varphi - \nu \Delta \varphi + \xi + \pi(\varphi) &= \gamma \vartheta - \rho \sigma \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\xi &\in \beta(\varphi) \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
\sigma &\in \sin \vartheta(\varphi - \varphi^*) \quad \text{a.e. in } Q \\
0 &= \vartheta_0 \quad \text{and } \varphi(0) = \varphi_0.
\end{align*}
$$

Here are our results on the well-posedness of the above problems:

**Theorem 2.1.** Assume $(2.1)-(2.3)$, $(2.16)$,

$$
\eta^* \in W \quad \text{and } \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Then, for every $\rho > 0$, Problem $(A)$ has at least a solution $(\vartheta, \varphi, \xi, \sigma)$ satisfying $(2.17)$–$(2.18)$ and the estimates

$$
\begin{align*}
\|\vartheta\|_{L^{\infty}(0, T; H) \cap L^{2}(0, T; V)} + \|\varphi\|_{H^{1}(0, T; H) \cap L^{2}(0, T; W)} \\
&\quad + \|\xi\|_{L^{2}(0, T; H)} + \|\sigma\|_{L^{\infty}(0, T; H)} \leq C_1 \\
\|\vartheta\|_{H^{1}(0, T; H) \cap L^{2}(0, T; W)} &\leq C_2 (\rho^{1/2} + 1)
\end{align*}
$$

---

**Corollary 2.1.** For $\rho = 0$ and $\varphi \in L^{\infty}(0, T; H)$, there is a unique function $\vartheta \in W$ such that

$$
\begin{align*}
\partial_t \vartheta(t) - \kappa \Delta \vartheta(t) + \xi(t) &= f \\
\partial_t \varphi(t) - \nu \Delta \varphi(t) + \xi(t) &\in \beta(\varphi(t)) \\
\text{and } \vartheta(0) &= \vartheta_0 \\
\varphi(0) &= \varphi_0,
\end{align*}
$$

where $\varphi \in W$.

---

**Corollary 2.2.** For $\rho = 0$ and $\varphi \in L^{\infty}(0, T; W)$, there is a unique function $\vartheta \in W$ such that

$$
\begin{align*}

\partial_t \varphi(t) - \nu \Delta \varphi(t) + \xi(t) &\in \beta(\varphi(t)) \\
\text{and } \vartheta(0) &= \vartheta_0 \\
\varphi(0) &= \varphi_0,
\end{align*}
$$

It follows that the above values of \(\rho^*\) and \( T^*\) depend continuously on the potentials and on the physical parameters of the systems. We also observe that the time \( T^*\) is roughly proportional to \( 1/\rho \) in both cases, whence it tends to zero as \(\rho\) tends to infinity, i.e., the sliding mode can be forced to start as soon as one desires by prescribing a sufficiently big factor \(\rho\) in front of the feedback control.

is one of the terms of total angular momentum.Close this comment box.The舵 thesis, also known as the steering problem, is a fundamental problem in control theory. It involves determining the optimal control input to steer a given vehicle from one equilibrium position to another while taking into account various constraints such as limitations on steering angle, steering wheel motion, and vehicle dynamics. The extreme value problem is the problem of finding the maximum or minimum value of a function subject to a constraint. In the context of steering, the objective function is usually the deviation from the desired trajectory, while the constraint is usually set by the limits of the steering angle or the steering wheel motion. The extreme value problem can be solved by maximizing or minimizing a function subject to a set of constraints. This problem has a wide range of applications in fields such as aerospace engineering, automotive engineering, and robotics.

The control problem is to design a control law that minimizes the deviation from the desired trajectory and satisfies the constraints. This is typically achieved through the application of linear quadratic control (LQR) techniques. LQR is a method for designing a control law that minimizes the expected long-term cost function, which in this case is the weighted sum of the state process and the constraint function. The state process is usually modeled as a linear system with a costate variable that represents the deviation from the desired trajectory. The optimization problem is usually formulated using the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, which is a partial differential equation that describes the optimal control strategy. The solution to the HJB equation can be expressed in terms of the value functions, which are linear operators that map the state process to its value.

The problem of steering can be extended to the problem of dynamic steering, which involves not only control action but also the dynamics of the vehicle. In the dynamic steering problem, the steering angle is controlled by a vector-valued function that maps the reference trajectory to the steering wheel deflection angle. The optimization problem becomes more complicated as the vehicle dynamics become non-linear. In such cases, the problem can be solved using advanced optimization techniques such as gradient-based methods and Pontryagin's minimum principle.

In conclusion, the problem of steering is a fundamental optimization problem that has many applications in various fields. The basic problem involves finding the optimal control action that minimizes the deviation from the desired trajectory while satisfying various constraints such as limits on steering angle or steering wheel motion. The solution to the problem can be expressed in terms of the value functions, which are linear operators that map the state process to its value.

\end{align*}
$$

where $k \Delta$ is set by the noise weight. The precision of a digital full-field source at base station travel time is then given as $\frac{\Delta_k^2}{10^3}.$

One such application is maximizing the inhibitory effect of the local $A(0)$ and $A'(0)$ signal from sources located within each model cell for a given time range, given the mean model efficiency.

The model can then be optimized with $\Pi = Ed+\int_0^2|\dot{\psi}(t)|\phi(t)dt$ and time-independent $E = F \phi$ off-time. This cost function is more general than $d+h$ distance-based norm because here we can only derive bounds, but not optimal solutions in all cases. To derive the optimal solution $t^*$, we may use Lagrangian multipliers as in N edeqte.

The periodic boundary requires solving several equations at each time in the source model. Via symmetrization, the boundary conditions on the first row and column of the forward model always yield quadratic relations, while for the first column and the first and last row the boundary condition equations take the form of a matrix equation. All boundary conditions not included in this equation are enforced by specific elements of $A(t)$ for which the column and row products within the current model boundary have predetermined values for derivations within this equation.

To ease the computational load of the Lagrangian formulation, one can consider time domain regularized solving by incorporating temporal space as smoothing in the cost function for equation (11) at each update step of the gradient scheme.
